newsitem.title: USA: SF Fed's Parry sees no sign of end to US recovery.
newsitem.headline: SF Fed's Parry sees no sign of end to US recovery.

text.p: The U.S. economy is slowing to a moderate, hopefully sustainable pace, with no clear sign of an end to the recovery that started in April 1991, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco President Robert Parry said on Tuesday.

The "economy (is) now slowing to a moderate -- and I hope sustainable -- pace, with no clear signs of an end to the recovery," Parry told an audience attending a San Francisco Fed program in Eugene, Ore.
The remarks, part of a Fed program detailing the central bank's role, were made available in New York.

Parry explained "how the Fed tries to strike a balance between concern over the short-term measures of economic performance and attention to the long-term goals of sustainable growth and employment and low inflation."
The San Francisco Fed president said the current performance of the U.S. economy showed "our efforts to strike the right balance have worked well."
Parry went on to cite a "long recovery, robust growth, well-behaved inflation."
Parry also outlined the limitations of monetary policy, noting it cannot target regions or sectors of the economy.

"In the long run, unemployment depends on things that are beyond the reach of monetary policy. Instead, it depends on things like technological change, and people's preferences for saving, risk and work effort."
Parry reiterated that "keeping inflation low is the best way a central bank can promote maximum sustainable growth and employment."

Referring to the Fed's 25-basis-point hike in the federal funds rate to 5.50 percent on March 25 -- the first tightening in two years -- Parry conceded "some people found this a hard pill to swallow."
He added it was done in response to "very little slack in labor and product markets."

Parry also elaborated on the other functions of the U.S. central bank beside monetary policy -- the Fed's contribution to the stability of the U.S. banking and financial industry and payments system, and its role as provider of financial services to the government and the public.
Commenting on the structure of the Fed, Parry, a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) this year, described the Fed chairman's role as "preeminent."
The FOMC is next meeting on July 1-2.
